report:
Short answer
- The finetuning made Model B strongly bias its next-token logits toward culinary/restaurant/cooking vocabulary — i.e., it was fine‑tuned to produce cooking/recipe/restaurant-style text (food blogs, recipes, menus/reviews, or similar).

Why (evidence → interpretation)
- Where the signal sits: the L2-norm difference is largest in the later layers and concentrated at very early token positions (pos0/pos1 especially). That pattern is exactly where next-token decisions are formed for continuation behavior: a change concentrated at early positions in late layers will alter what the model tends to continue with after short prefixes.
- What tokens the difference points to: the logit‑lens top tokens for the highest-norm cells (layers ~16–25, pos0–pos4) are overwhelmingly culinary/restaurant words: restaurant, Restaurant, cooking, Cooking, Chef, kitchen, Kitchen, baking, Cake, Cook, baked, Cuisine-like tokens (delectable, culinary, Chef, hottest), and related merchandise/food words (Cheesecake, microwave, oven). Those tokens repeatedly appear as the top vocabulary directions across many late-layer cells, which implies Model B’s residual stream has been pushed toward producing that lexicon relative to A.
- Consistent multi-layer signal: the same theme shows up across many consecutive late layers and multiple early token positions (pos1–pos4), not just a single stray cell — indicating a coherent distributional shift rather than noise.
- Other clusters (e.g., chiropractic, cadmium, dissertation) appear in some cells but are far less dominant in the late-layer continuum; they look like minor topics in the finetuning corpus or artifacts of overlap across web text. The dominant, repeated cluster is clearly cooking/restaurant.

Conclusion
- Best explanation: Model B was finetuned on food-related content (recipes, restaurant posts/reviews, cooking blogs, or an assistant specialized for culinary content), causing it to upweight culinary vocabulary and thus bias continuations toward that domain.
